# References & Further Reading {.unnumbered}

The histories in this book draw on food scholarship, culinary writing, and the
living knowledge of the cooks who keep these traditions. The works below are good
next stops if you want to go deeper. Origin stories for folk dishes are contested
by nature — where sources disagree, this book tries to say so.

::: {#refs}
:::

## A few great places to keep reading

- **Jessica B. Harris**, *High on the Hog* — the African diaspora's foundational
  role in American (and Atlantic) rice cookery.
- **Naomi Duguid & Jeffrey Alford**, *Seductions of Rice* — a global tour of rice
  cultures and techniques.
- **Najmieh Batmanglij**, *Food of Life* — the definitive English-language work on
  Persian rice cookery and *tahdig*.
- **Claudia Roden**, *The New Book of Middle Eastern Food* — essential on the
  spiced-rice traditions of the Levant and Gulf.
- On **jollof** and West African rice: the scholarship tracing rice from the Niger
  Delta and the Senegambian Wolof origins of the dish.

::: {.callout-note}
Found a better source, or think we got a history wrong? The
[Contributing](chapters/contributing.qmd) chapter explains how to send a
correction — with a citation.
:::
